newsitem.title: CHINA: China said to promise Hong Kong polls by mid-1998.
newsitem.headline: China said to promise Hong Kong polls by mid-1998.

text.p: China has promised Hong Kong will hold elections for a new legislature by mid-1998, Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy said on Wednesday.
Axworthy told reporters that Chinese officials advised him that elections for Hong Kong's Legislative Council would be held "before July 1 next year".

The Canadian foreign minister, who met Chinese Premier Li Peng, Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and top official for Hong Kong Lu Ping on Wednesday, said there was no indication of who would be entitled to vote or how many seats would be directly elected.
This would be determined after Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty on July 1 under a Sino-British accord, Axworthy said.
China has said it will dismantle Hong Kong's elected legislature and replace it with an appointed provisional body once it regains sovereignty.

Beijing has come under criticism from democratic activists in the territory and from the United States and Britain. It has also come under pressure to hold early elections to replace the appointed provisional body.
Under a Sino-British accord on Hong Kong signed in 1984, China has pledged to give the territory a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the transfer of power.
Both Beijing and officials in Hong Kong's incoming administration have said the provisional legislature will last for just one year, but have yet to specify a date for new polls.

A Beijing-appointed committee is conducting a consultation exercise in Hong Kong on new electoral methods to replace the reformed rules used in the 1995 polls that resulted in Hong Kong's first-ever fully elected legislature. China rejected the reformed rules, saying they violated previous Sino-British agreements.
Axworthy also said human rights in China were discussed in his meetings with Chinese officials.
"We have given them a list" of names, he said, without identifying any of the people.
China has jailed or exiled most of its small band of active political dissidents.
Canada and China also signed an agreement to train senior Chinese judges as well as a pact on the buying of land for diplomatic purchases by the two countries.
